4.1.title: Attack Types — Identification & Mitigation
rows: Single attacker floods target with traffic or exploits vulnerability to exhaust resources
Rate limiting, firewall ACLs, null routing attack source
Botnet of thousands of compromised hosts floods target simultaneously
Anti-DDoS scrubbing service (Cloudflare, AWS Shield), upstream filtering
Attacker positions between two hosts — intercepts and optionally modifies traffic
Encrypt all traffic (TLS/IPsec), certificate pinning, mutual authentication
Attacker sends gratuitous ARPs to map victim IPs to attacker's MAC — intercepts LAN traffic
Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI), static ARP entries for critical hosts
Corrupt DNS cache or intercept DNS responses — redirect users to malicious sites
DNSSEC, encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT), use trusted resolvers
Attacker runs unauthorised DHCP server — assigns malicious default gateway/DNS
DHCP snooping — designate trusted DHCP ports only
Attacker sets up fake AP with same SSID — users connect, traffic intercepted
802.1X Enterprise auth (rogue can't replicate), wireless IDS, RF monitoring
Attacker sends spoofed deauth frames to disconnect clients from legitimate AP
Double-tagging or DTP exploit to jump to another VLAN
Change native VLAN, disable DTP, use dedicated unused native VLAN
Attacker captures and retransmits valid authentication traffic
Session tokens, timestamps, nonces in authentication protocols
Try a few common passwords against many accounts — avoids lockout thresholds
Account lockout after N attempts, MFA, strong password policy
Systematically try all possible passwords against one account
Account lockout, MFA, long complex passwords, rate limiting
Pre-computed hash-to-plaintext lookup table for cracking password hashes
Salt passwords before hashing — salting defeats rainbow tables entirely
key_points: ARP poisoning → On-path/MITM at Layer 2. Mitigation: DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection).
DNS poisoning → redirect at Layer 7. Mitigation: DNSSEC validates DNS responses cryptographically.
Rogue DHCP → gives clients malicious gateway. Mitigation: DHCP snooping (trust only uplink port).
Evil twin vs rogue AP: rogue = unauthorised AP on your network. Evil twin = fake AP mimicking your SSID.
DDoS types: Volumetric (bandwidth flood), Protocol (SYN flood, Smurf — exploits L3/L4), Application (HTTP flood, Slowloris — L7).
Salt defeats rainbow tables — even same passwords produce different hashes per-user.

4.1.title: Social Engineering Attacks
rows: Mass email impersonating trusted entity — generic, sent to many
Fake PayPal email asking all users to 'verify account'
Targeted phishing — researched and personalised for specific victim
Email to CFO from 'CEO' requesting urgent wire transfer
Fake legal subpoena email sent to CEO
Voice/phone phishing — caller impersonates IT helpdesk, bank, IRS
'This is Microsoft Support — your PC is infected, give us access'
SMS phishing — text message with malicious link or pretexting
Text: 'Your package is held — click here to confirm delivery'
Creating a fabricated scenario to extract information
Attacker pretends to be an auditor needing network credentials
Following an authorised person through a secured door without authenticating
Attacker carries boxes and walks in behind badge-access employee
Leaving infected USB drives in visible locations for victims to plug in
USB labelled 'Payroll Q4 2024' left in company car park
key_points: Phishing is generic (mass). Spear phishing is targeted. Whaling targets executives specifically.
Vishing = Voice. Smishing = SMS. Phishing = Email. Know the prefix.
Social engineering exploits HUMANS, not technology — technical controls don't fully prevent it.
Key defence: security awareness training — users recognise and report attempts.
Pretexting = the story the attacker tells to justify their request for access/info.
Tailgating defence: mantrap/airlock, badge + PIN, security awareness training to challenge strangers.

4.1.title: DDoS Attack Categories & Threat Actors
rows: Overwhelm bandwidth — huge traffic volume (Gbps scale)
UDP flood, ICMP flood, DNS amplification
Exhaust state tables on firewalls/routers — not just bandwidth
SYN flood (half-open TCP connections), Smurf attack
Exhaust server resources with seemingly valid requests
HTTP GET flood, Slowloris (holds connections open), DNS query flood
Government-sponsored, highly skilled, long-term APT campaigns
Ideologically motivated — embarrass or disrupt target
Current or former employee with legitimate access
Disgruntled employee exfiltrating data or sabotaging systems
Low skill — uses existing tools/exploits without understanding them
Runs downloaded DDoS tools against targets
Financially motivated — ransomware, data theft, fraud
key_points: DNS amplification: small query → large response sent to spoofed victim IP. Amplification factor up to 50x.
SYN flood: send many SYN packets without completing handshake — exhausts server's half-open connection table.
Mitigation for SYN flood: SYN cookies (server doesn't allocate state until handshake complete).
APT (Advanced Persistent Threat): long-term, stealthy compromise — often nation-state sponsored.
Insider threat: hardest to detect — has legitimate credentials. Defence: least privilege, DLP, audit logs.
Script kiddies: unsophisticated but can still cause damage with off-the-shelf tools.

4.2.title: Firewall Types — Full Comparison
rows: Src/Dst IP, port, protocol per packet
Cannot validate return traffic; easily spoofed
App ID, User ID, SSL decryption, IPS, threat intel
Higher cost; SSL inspection adds latency; complex config
Web traffic only — not general purpose
FW + IPS + AV + Web filter + VPN + DLP in one box
Single point of failure; performance impact; SMB-focused
key_points: Stateless = no memory of connections. Stateful = tracks session state (syn/established/fin).
NGFW adds App-ID (identifies app regardless of port) and User-ID beyond stateful.
WAF: specifically defends web apps against SQLi, XSS, path traversal — placed in front of web servers.
UTM: one appliance for everything — cost-effective for small business but can bottleneck.
Implicit deny: firewall drops anything not explicitly permitted. Always the last rule.
DMZ: screened subnet between two firewalls — public-facing servers here (web, mail, DNS).

4.2.title: IDS vs IPS and Network Segmentation
rows: DETECTS and ALERTS — passive, out-of-band or tap mode
Cannot block traffic. False positive = alert on legitimate traffic. No latency added.
DETECTS and BLOCKS — active, inline mode
Sits in the traffic path. False positive = drops legitimate traffic. Adds small latency.
Host-based IDS/IPS — agent installed on endpoint
Monitors OS calls, file changes, running processes on the host itself.
Screened subnet between untrusted internet and trusted internal network
Public-facing servers (web, email, DNS) placed here. Internet can reach DMZ; DMZ cannot initiate to internal.
Synonym for DMZ — subnet accessible from both internet and internal, but restricted
Typically between two firewalls: external FW faces internet, internal FW protects LAN.
Decoy system designed to attract attackers — logs their techniques
No real data. Alerts admins to active intrusion attempts. Honeynets = multiple honeypots.
Hardened, audited gateway to reach sensitive internal systems
Admins connect to bastion first, then SSH/RDP from there to internal servers.
Granular network segmentation — per-workload firewall policies (East-West traffic control)
Software-defined; used in data centres/cloud. Limits lateral movement if one host is compromised.
key_points: IDS = detect only. IPS = detect + block. IPS must be inline; IDS can be tap/span.
IPS false positive risk: blocks legitimate traffic — tune signatures carefully.
DMZ: two-firewall design — outer FW (internet→DMZ), inner FW (DMZ→LAN). Only DMZ servers are reachable from internet.
Honeypot: zero legitimate traffic expected — any access = suspicious. High signal-to-noise ratio for alerts.
Zero Trust: 'never trust, always verify' — no implicit trust based on network location. Every access request authenticated/authorized.
Defense in depth: multiple overlapping security layers — compromising one layer doesn't mean full compromise.

4.3.title: VPN Types — Site-to-Site vs Remote Access
rows: Permanently connect two office networks over internet
Router/firewall handles VPN — transparent to end users. Always-on.
Individual users connect to corporate network from anywhere
Client software on endpoint. User authenticates to connect.
Works through firewalls (port 443 usually open). Clientless option via browser.
More complex setup. Better performance. Blocked by some firewalls (UDP 500/4500).
No encryption by default — combine with IPsec for security.
Only corporate traffic goes through VPN — internet goes direct
Reduces VPN load but internet traffic bypasses corporate security controls.
key_points: SSL/TLS VPN advantage: uses HTTPS port 443 — rarely blocked by firewalls. Easy for remote users.
IPsec advantage: stronger performance for site-to-site. Uses UDP 500 (IKE), UDP 4500 (NAT traversal).
Full tunnel: ALL traffic through VPN (including internet) — more secure but higher load on VPN gateway.
Split tunnel: only LAN traffic through VPN — internet bypasses VPN. Security risk: endpoint not protected by corporate controls.
GRE alone = no security. GRE + IPsec = encrypted tunnel that can carry routing protocols.
Always-on VPN: endpoint is always connected to corporate network — reduces attack surface on remote devices.

4.3.title: IPsec — Protocols, Modes, and Key Exchange
rows: IP protocol 51. Verifies packet was not tampered with. Does NOT hide content.
IP protocol 50. Encrypts payload. Used in almost all deployments.
Encrypts payload only — original IP header preserved
Used for host-to-host VPNs. Endpoints must be VPN endpoints.
Encrypts entire original packet + adds new outer IP header
Used for network-to-network (site-to-site) VPNs. Standard for most VPNs.
Establishes secure channel for Phase 2 negotiation. Diffie-Hellman key exchange.
Creates ISAKMP SA (management tunnel). Main mode (6 msgs) or Aggressive mode (3 msgs).
Negotiates the actual IPsec tunnel parameters (encryption, hashing, lifetime)
Creates IPsec SA (data tunnel). Uses PFS optionally.
New Diffie-Hellman exchange for each session — compromise of one key doesn't expose others
Prevents decryption of past sessions if long-term keys are later compromised.
key_points: AH = integrity only (no encryption). ESP = encryption + integrity. Use ESP.
Transport mode: encrypt payload only (host-to-host). Tunnel mode: encrypt entire packet (network-to-network).
IKE Phase 1 = management tunnel (authenticate peers). Phase 2 = data tunnel (IPsec SA).
UDP 500 = IKE/ISAKMP. UDP 4500 = IPsec NAT traversal (encapsulates ESP in UDP).
DH (Diffie-Hellman): allows two parties to establish shared secret over insecure channel. Basis of IKE.
PFS: use it. Without PFS, compromise of the long-term key can decrypt ALL past traffic.

4.3.title: PKI, Certificates, and Encryption
rows: Framework for issuing, managing, and revoking digital certificates
Enables trust in public keys via chain of trust to a trusted CA.
Trusted entity that signs and issues digital certificates
Root CA → Intermediate CA → End-entity cert. Root CA self-signed.
Binds a public key to an identity, signed by CA
Contains: subject, issuer, public key, validity period, SAN, serial number.
Request submitted to CA containing public key + identity info
CA signs the CSR → issues certificate. Private key never leaves the requester.
Published list of revoked certificate serial numbers
Checked by clients to detect revoked certs. Can be stale — updated periodically.
Client queries OCSP responder for cert status: good/revoked/unknown. Faster than CRL.
Same key encrypts and decrypts — fast
AES-128/256 (block cipher). Used for bulk data encryption.
Public key encrypts; private key decrypts (or vice versa for signatures)
RSA, ECC. Slower. Used for key exchange, signatures, certificates.
Protocol securing communications — record protocol + handshake protocol
TLS 1.3 current standard. Negotiates cipher suite, exchanges keys, authenticates server (and optionally client).
key_points: TLS handshake: client hello → server hello + cert → client verifies cert → key exchange → symmetric session key established.
Certificate chain: trust flows Root CA → Intermediate CA → End-entity cert. Root CA must be trusted by client.
CRL vs OCSP: CRL = list (download whole list). OCSP = per-cert query (real-time, more efficient).
OCSP stapling: server fetches OCSP response and 'staples' it to TLS handshake — client doesn't need to query OCSP separately.
AES (symmetric) for bulk data. RSA/ECDH (asymmetric) for key exchange. Hybrid approach used in TLS.
Self-signed certificate: signed by same entity that issued it — not trusted by others without explicit import.

4.4.title: AAA — RADIUS vs TACACS+
rows: Combines Authentication + Authorization in one response
key_points: RADIUS = UDP, encrypts only password. TACACS+ = TCP, encrypts everything.
RADIUS best for network access (802.1X, VPN). TACACS+ best for device admin (SSH to router).
AAA: Authentication (who are you?), Authorization (what can you do?), Accounting (what did you do?).
RADIUS ports: UDP 1812 (auth) / 1813 (accounting). Old: 1645/1646. Know both.
TACACS+ TCP 49. TCP = reliable delivery — important for device management sessions.
EAP runs over 802.1X — RADIUS is the backend that processes EAP authentication.

4.4.title: Layer 2 Security — DHCP Snooping, DAI, Port Security
rows: Designates switch ports as 'trusted' (uplink to real DHCP server) or 'untrusted' (access ports). DHCP offers on untrusted ports are dropped.
Uses DHCP snooping binding table to validate ARP packets. ARP replies on untrusted ports checked — invalid = dropped.
Validates source IP on untrusted ports against DHCP snooping binding table. Prevents hosts from spoofing another host's IP.
Limits number of MAC addresses on an access port. Violation modes: Protect (drop), Restrict (drop + log), Shutdown (err-disable port).
Port security variant — first learned MAC is stored in config automatically. Only that MAC allowed unless manually changed.
Rate-limits broadcast, multicast, or unicast traffic per port. Activates when threshold exceeded (drops or shuts port).
key_points: DHCP snooping must be enabled BEFORE DAI — DAI relies on the DHCP snooping binding table.
Port security violation modes: Protect (silent drop), Restrict (drop + SNMP alert), Shutdown (err-disable — port goes down). Default = Shutdown.
Sticky MAC: learned dynamically but saved to running-config. Survives reboot if saved to startup-config.
DAI: all ports untrusted by default — only trunk/uplink ports should be trusted.
IP Source Guard: stops hosts from using IP addresses not assigned to them via DHCP.
Storm control: prevents a broadcast storm from taking down the entire segment — sets threshold (packets/sec or %).

4.4.title: ACLs and 802.1X / NAC
4.4.body:
ACCESS CONTROL LISTS (ACLs):
  Standard ACL: matches SOURCE IP only. Numbered 1–99 or 1300–1999.
  Extended ACL: matches src IP + dst IP + protocol + src/dst port. Numbered 100–199 or 2000–2699.

  PLACEMENT RULE:
    Extended ACL → as CLOSE to SOURCE as possible (blocks traffic early)
    Standard ACL → as CLOSE to DESTINATION as possible (only matches src IP, so must be near dest to avoid over-blocking)

  ACL PROCESSING:
    Top-down, first-match wins. Implicit deny at end = any traffic not explicitly permitted is dropped.
    Always add explicit 'permit ip any any' at bottom if you want to allow everything else.

802.1X PORT-BASED ACCESS CONTROL:
  Supplicant (client) → Authenticator (switch/AP) → Authentication Server (RADIUS)
  EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) is the framework used.
  Port starts in unauthorised state — only 802.1X traffic allowed.
  On RADIUS Accept: port moves to authorised state — full network access granted.
  On RADIUS Reject: port stays blocked (or placed in guest VLAN if configured).

NAC (Network Access Control):
  Checks endpoint posture before granting network access — is antivirus up to date? Patches current? Compliant?
  Non-compliant endpoints quarantined to remediation VLAN.
key_points: Standard ACL near destination. Extended ACL near source.
Implicit deny: last rule in every ACL — drops anything not matched above. Often the reason traffic is blocked.
802.1X requires: supplicant (client + EAP software), authenticator (switch with 802.1X enabled), RADIUS server.
NAC = posture assessment before access. Quarantine VLAN for non-compliant hosts.
ACL numbers: standard = 1–99. Extended = 100–199. Named ACLs also supported.
ACE (Access Control Entry): individual line in an ACL. Processed top to bottom — order matters.
